clinicalPearls: Umbrella term for disorders of telomere maintenance producing abnormally short telomeres; it encompasses dyskeratosis congenita and its severe variants (Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson, Revesz and Coats plus syndromes).

Caused by variants in telomere-maintenance genes including TERT, TERC, DKC1, TINF2, RTEL1, PARN, NAF1, NOP10, NHP2, WRAP53, ACD, CTC1 and STN1; inheritance may be X-linked (DKC1), autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive.
The classic dyskeratosis congenita mucocutaneous triad is nail dystrophy, oral leucoplakia and reticulate skin pigmentation, but it is frequently incomplete or absent, especially in adults.
Bone marrow failure with single or multilineage cytopenias and aplastic anaemia is a leading cause of early morbidity and mortality.
Adult presentations are often cryptic: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, unexplained cirrhosis or apparently isolated cytopenias, sometimes with premature greying of hair.
Genetic anticipation, with earlier onset and greater severity in successive generations, reflects progressive telomere shortening.
There is a high lifetime risk of myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukaemia and squamous cell carcinomas of the head and neck and anogenital region.
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating abnormally short leucocyte telomeres (flow-FISH), interpreted against age-matched values, together with genetic testing.
reference.pathophysiology: Telomeres are repetitive TTAGGG nucleoprotein caps that protect chromosome ends. They are maintained by the telomerase enzyme complex (the catalytic reverse transcriptase TERT, the RNA template TERC, and dyskerin/DKC1 with NOP10, NHP2 and GAR1 that stabilise TERC), by telomerase biogenesis and trafficking factors (WRAP53/TCAB1, PARN and NAF1), by the shelterin complex (including TINF2/TIN2 and ACD/TPP1) that caps the ends and recruits telomerase, and by the CST complex (CTC1-STN1-TEN1) that supports replication of the telomeric C-strand. Loss-of-function or dominant-negative variants in these genes accelerate telomere attrition; once telomeres become critically short they trigger a DNA-damage response leading to cellular senescence or apoptosis, depleting rapidly dividing stem-cell compartments. This preferentially affects haematopoietic stem cells (marrow failure), alveolar and airway epithelium (pulmonary fibrosis), hepatocytes and vascular endothelium (liver disease) and skin and mucosa, while genomic instability arising from dysfunctional telomeres underlies the elevated cancer risk.
additionalDifferentials: Fanconi anaemia and other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (Shwachman-Diamond, Diamond-Blackfan anaemia)
Acquired aplastic anaemia and idiopathic myelodysplastic syndrome
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis without a recognised telomere cause
Poikiloderma syndromes such as Rothmund-Thomson syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Leucocyte telomere length by flow-FISH, interpreted against age-matched percentiles
Targeted telomere-gene panel or whole-exome sequencing
Full blood count with reticulocytes and bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics
Chromosome breakage testing to exclude Fanconi anaemia
High-resolution chest CT and pulmonary function tests
Liver function tests with hepatic imaging and elastography
Structured surveillance for myelodysplastic syndrome, leukaemia and mucosal squamous cell carcinoma
redFlags: New or progressive cytopenias or other features of marrow failure
Progressive breathlessness or radiological pulmonary fibrosis
Signs of portal hypertension or hepatopulmonary syndrome
New oral, anogenital or cutaneous lesions suspicious for squamous cell carcinoma
Severe infantile presentation with cerebellar hypoplasia and immunodeficiency suggesting Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome
reference.prognosis: Highly variable, ranging from early childhood death in severe infantile forms to adult-onset organ fibrosis. Overall life expectancy is reduced, driven by marrow failure, pulmonary and hepatic fibrosis and malignancy.
pitfalls: Expecting the full mucocutaneous triad; many patients, particularly adults, lack the classic skin and nail findings
Attributing pulmonary fibrosis or cirrhosis to another cause and missing the underlying telomeropathy
Using standard-intensity conditioning for haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which is poorly tolerated; reduced-intensity approaches are preferred
Overlooking at-risk relatives who need counselling and telomere-aware screening
Relying solely on telomere length, since results may fall within the normal range for certain genotypes, so genetic testing remains essential
references: Inherited bone marrow failure syndrome guidelines
Dyskeratosis congenita and telomere biology disorder reviews
management: Treat bone marrow failure with androgen therapy such as danazol to stimulate residual marrow, reserving allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation for severe or transfusion-dependent cytopenias
Use reduced-intensity conditioning for transplantation because these patients are exquisitely sensitive to DNA-damaging chemotherapy and radiotherapy
Manage pulmonary fibrosis with best supportive respiratory care and lung transplantation, and consider liver transplantation for progressive hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis
Provide transfusion and infection support for cytopenias using leucodepleted, irradiated blood products, with iron chelation where transfusion burden is high
Advise strict avoidance of telomere- and DNA-damaging exposures including smoking, excess alcohol and unnecessary radiation
Institute lifelong surveillance for the associated malignancies including myelodysplasia, acute leukaemia and squamous cell carcinomas, with regular mucocutaneous, marrow and imaging review
Offer genetic counselling and family screening including telomere-length testing, given the heritable disorder that shows genetic anticipation
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across haematology, respiratory medicine, hepatology and clinical genetics
